units.unit: The student wants to understand the debate over rent control for subdivided flats in Hong Kong.
The student asks for sources on how the caps work and who they affect.
The student wants to start with how the caps actually work.
The student is trying to figure out whether a rent cap keeps rents down or just changes who gets in and who is pushed out.
The student wants the theory of how caps work, the Berlin comparison, and the stock data.
The student wants to look at the enforcement angle.
The student wants to look at what tenants themselves say would help most.
The student wants to do enforcement first.
The student wants a source on whether authorities could catch landlords who break the rules, covering inspection capacity and where enforcement falls short.
The student wants enforcement capacity, tenants' own preferences, and a first-person account.
The student reached the thesis by working through the archive rather than starting with it.
The first- versus second-generation distinction in D6 made the student realize the 2021 ordinance only capped increases within tenancies and never touched initial rents.
Because the ordinance never touched initial rents, the stable stock numbers do not prove a hard cap is safe.
The working paper's contraction estimates applied specifically to a binding cap on initial rents.
The thesis statement followed from the evidence instead of coming first.
The interview with Mr Chan and the NGO survey both show tenants care most about the public-housing queue and security, not the rent level.
The rent started to look like a symptom of a deeper problem.
The working paper's point that a cap mainly shifts costs onto new entrants.
The cap never touches the real constraint, which is the queue.
The working paper's model shows a 15 percent cut in initial rents would block 3,000 to 4,000 households a year from entering the segment, mostly new arrivals and newly formed households.
The primer's point that these groups are the segment's core tenants.
The people shut out are exactly the ones with the fewest alternatives.
The student framed it as the households most in need bearing the cost of contraction.
Source D1 describes how the 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance only capped rent increases within an existing tenancy and did not regulate the initial rent at the start of a new one.
The student used it in paragraph 3 because it sets up the first- versus second-generation distinction from D6p2.
The point was not in earlier Room work; the student added it later once D6 framed the ordinance as a second-generation, non-binding control.
The student got the figure from source D2 and added it during drafting rather than from earlier Room discussion.
The student used it to show stock kept growing under the 2021 ordinance.
The student argues the growth is misleading because the cap wasn't binding on initial rents.
It is the student's own reading of the source, not something from the tutor's feedback.
